pos: n. (that which makes a thing what it is; in theology, the divine being itself, one and undivided)
etymology: Latin essentia, from esse, to be — coined to render the Greek ousia, being. The word entered Christian theology at Nicaea, where the Son was confessed of one substance with the Father.
biblical_def: Essence is what a thing is, as distinguished from what it has and what it does. Of God the term names His being itself, which He declares of Himself without reference to anything outside Him: “I AM THAT I AM” (Exo 3:14). That being is underived — “as the Father hath life in himself; so hath he given to the Son to have life in himself” (John 5:26) — and it is one: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD” (Deu 6:4). In Him “we live, and move, and have our being” (Act 17:28), which is the exact reverse: creatures have their being in Him, and He has His in Himself.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines essence as the nature, substance, or being of any thing; that which constitutes or marks the particular nature of a being or substance; formal existence.
webster_full: ESSENCE, n. That which constitutes the particular nature of a being or substance, or of a genus, and which distinguishes it from all others.
2. Formal existence; that which makes any thing to be what it is; or rather the peculiar nature of a thing; the very substance.
3. Existence; the quality of being.
4. A being; an existent person.
scriptures: Exo 3:14
And God said unto Moses, I AM THAT I AM: and he said, Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you.
Deu 6:4
Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD:
John 5:26
For as the Father hath life in himself; so hath he given to the Son to have life in himself;
For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring.
Heb 1:3

Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high;
corruption_summary: God is defined by what He does for us, and Exodus 3:14 gives a name that says nothing about us at all.
corruption_paragraphs: The name given at the bush is the most reserved sentence in Scripture. Moses asks what he shall say when the people ask the name of the God of their fathers, and the answer contains no attribute, no promise, and no relation: I AM THAT I AM. God defines Himself by Himself. Every modern definition that begins with human need — God is whatever meets the deepest longing, God is the ground of my meaning — has started at the far end of the sentence and will never arrive at the near one, because a being defined by its usefulness to me is by definition not the being of Exodus 3.

The doctrine that follows is the one the creeds fought over: that Father, Son and Holy Ghost are one in essence and three in person — not three parts of God, not three modes of one person, not three gods. The Second London Confession puts it in a sentence that has to be read slowly: in this divine and infinite Being there are three subsistences, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, of one substance, power and eternity. The word essence is doing necessary work there. Remove it and the Trinity becomes either a committee or a costume change, and both have been tried.

There is a devotional corruption too, which is to treat the doctrine of the divine essence as cold and to prefer a warmer God who is more like us. Scripture does not offer the trade. The comfort of Malachi 3:6 — I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed — is a comfort that runs directly out of the essence: it is precisely because His being does not shift that the covenant holds and the sons of Jacob survive. A God near enough to be changed by us would be too small to keep anyone.
roots_summary: Hebrew ehyeh asher ehyeh (H1961), I AM THAT I AM; echad (H259), one; Greek ousia, being, essence; hupostasis (G5287), substance, person.
roots_lines: Hebrew ehyeh asher ehyeh (H1961) — I AM THAT I AM; Exodus 3:14, whence the covenant name.
Hebrew echad (H259) — one; Deuteronomy 6:4, the Shema.
Greek hupostasis (G5287) — substance, the express image of his person; Hebrews 1:3, 11:1.
usage: “I AM THAT I AM” — a name with no reference to us in it.
“As the Father hath life in himself” — being underived, and given to the Son.
“In him we live, and move, and have our being” — the creature's being is on loan.

pos: n. (the divine nature; Godhead; that which belongs to God alone)
etymology: Latin deitas, coined by Augustine to render the Greek theotes; the Authorized Version renders that Greek word Godhead.
biblical_def: Deity is the divine nature itself, and the Authorized Version's word for it is Godhead. Paul says of Christ, “in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily” (Col 2:9); of the Creator's evidence in the world, “his eternal power and Godhead” (Rom 1:20); and to the Athenians, “we ought not to think that the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man's device” (Act 17:29). What belongs to Deity alone is worship: “Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve” (Mat 4:10) — which is why Thomas's confession before the risen Christ, “My Lord and my God” (John 20:28), is received rather than corrected.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines deity as godhead; divinity; the nature and essence of the Supreme Being; and, in a lower sense, a fabulous god, an idol.
webster_full: DEITY, n. Godhead; divinity; the nature and essence of the Supreme Being.
2. God; the Supreme Being, or infinite self-existent Spirit.
3. A fabulous god; an idol; a person or thing deified or highly honored.
scriptures: Col 2:9
For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.
Rom 1:20
For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse:
Forasmuch then as we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man's device.
John 20:28
And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God.
Mat 4:10
Then saith Jesus unto him, Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve.
corruption_summary: Christ is called divine in a sense that would fit a saint, and Colossians says all the fulness of the Godhead dwells in Him bodily.
corruption_paragraphs: The liberal formula is that Jesus was divine, and it is designed to be inaudible: divine can mean godlike, exalted, uniquely conscious of God, the highest instance of what is in all of us. Colossians 2:9 closes every one of those doors with three words. Not divinity but the fulness of the Godhead; not partially but all of it; not in idea but bodily. Whatever it is that makes God God dwells in the man Christ Jesus completely and in a body, and the verse was written to a church being told it needed something further.

The evidence that the apostles meant deity in the strict sense is not a proof-text but a reflex. Angels refuse worship — “See thou do it not… worship God” (Rev 22:9) — and Peter lifts up Cornelius from his feet, and Paul and Barnabas rend their clothes at Lystra. Christ never once refuses it. He receives it from the leper, the ruler, the healed blind man, the disciples in the ship, and finally from Thomas, whose confession is the highest in the Gospels and is answered not by a correction but by a beatitude on those who will believe without seeing.

Romans 1:20 shows the other use of the word and it is a warning: the eternal power and Godhead are clearly seen from the creation, so that men are without excuse — and verse 23 says what they did with the knowledge, changing the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image. Deity is the one property that cannot be transferred, and every idolatry is an attempt to transfer it. Acts 17:29 states the impossibility with a kind of contempt for the workmanship: the Godhead is not like gold or silver graven by art and man's device.
roots_summary: Greek theotes (G2320), deity, the state of being God; theiotes (G2305), divinity, divine nature as displayed; to theion (G2304), the Godhead.
roots_lines: Greek theotes (G2320) — Godhead, deity; Colossians 2:9 only — the strongest of the three.
Greek theiotes (G2305) — Godhead, divinity as seen in creation; Romans 1:20 only.
Greek to theion (G2304) — the Godhead; Acts 17:29 only.
usage: “All the fulness of the Godhead bodily” — not divinity, and not partially.
“My Lord and my God” — received, not corrected.
“The Godhead is like unto gold” — the one property no image can carry.

pos: adj. (not capable of change; rendering Greek ametathetos)
etymology: Latin immutabilis, from in, not, and mutare, to change. Hebrews uses the Greek of a thing that cannot be transposed or set aside.
biblical_def: God swore by Himself to Abraham, “willing more abundantly to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel”, and confirmed it by an oath, “that by two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation” (Heb 6:17–18). The ground is His own declaration: “I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed” (Mal 3:6); “with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning” (Jas 1:17); “they shall perish, but thou shalt endure… thou art the same, and thy years shall have no end” (Psa 102:26–27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines immutable as invariable; unalterable; not capable or susceptible of change.
webster_full: IMMUTABLE, a. Invariable; unalterable; not capable or susceptible of change. The Deity is immutable.
scriptures: Heb 6:17
Wherein God, willing more abundantly to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, confirmed it by an oath:
Heb 6:18
That by two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation, who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us:
Mal 3:6
For I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed.
Jas 1:17
Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.
But thou art the same, and thy years shall have no end.
corruption_summary: Immutability is heard as coldness, and Hebrews offers it as the ground of a strong consolation.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 6:18 does not present the doctrine as an abstraction. Two immutable things — the promise and the oath — are given for a stated purpose: that we might have a strong consolation, who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us. The unchangeableness is pastoral before it is metaphysical. A God who could change His mind about the covenant would leave every promise provisional, and the writer's argument is that the heirs may hold an anchor sure and stedfast precisely because the One who swore cannot become someone else.

Malachi 3:6 shows the doctrine doing the same work in the other direction: I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed. The people addressed had been robbing God of tithes and wearying Him with words, and the reason they are still alive is not their improvement but His constancy. Immutability is therefore not indifference; it is what keeps mercy from expiring while a man is still in his sin.

The modern objection is that a changeless God cannot really be moved — cannot grieve, cannot repent, cannot answer prayer. Scripture speaks freely of God repenting and being grieved, and the older divines answered by distinguishing what God is from how He deals: His being, purpose and character do not alter, while His dealings with men alter as men alter, which the Scriptures describe in the language men can follow. Jonah's Nineveh is the test case, and the change there is in Nineveh. The threat was real, the repentance was real, and the God who spared the city was the same God who had sent the prophet.
roots_summary: Greek ametathetos (G276), unchangeable, not to be transposed; parallage (G3883), variation; alloioo; Hebrew shanah (H8138), to change.
roots_lines: Greek ametathetos (G276) — immutable, unchangeable; Hebrews 6:17–18 only.
Greek parallage (G3883) — variation, variableness; James 1:17 only, with trope, shadow of turning.
Hebrew shanah (H8138) — to change; Malachi 3:6; and hu, thou art the same; Psalm 102:27.
usage: “Two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie” — given for a strong consolation.
“I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed” — why the sinner is still alive.
“No variableness, neither shadow of turning” — not even the shadow that a turning would cast.

pos: adj. (not able to be contained or fully grasped; of God, exceeding the creature's compass)
etymology: Latin incomprehensibilis, from in, not, and comprehendere, to seize together. The theological sense is not that God is unknowable but that He cannot be encompassed — the creature cannot get his arms round Him.
biblical_def: Zophar asks the question the doctrine answers: “Canst thou by searching find out God? canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection?” (Job 11:7). Isaiah: “there is no searching of his understanding” (Isa 40:28). The psalmist: “Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised; and his greatness is unsearchable” (Psa 145:3). Paul, at the end of eleven chapters of argument: “O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!” (Rom 11:33). Yet He is truly known where He has spoken: “The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children” (Deu 29:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines incomprehensible as that cannot be comprehended or understood; beyond the reach of human intellect; inconceivable; not to be contained.
webster_full: INCOMPREHENSIBLE, a. That cannot be comprehended or understood; beyond the reach of human intellect; inconceivable.
2. Not to be contained; boundless; immense; as the incomprehensible God.
scriptures: Job 11:7
Canst thou by searching find out God? canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection?
Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary? there is no searching of his understanding.
Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised; and his greatness is unsearchable.
O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!
The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law.
corruption_summary: Incomprehensible is taken to mean unknowable, and Deuteronomy 29:29 divides the secret things from the revealed and gives the revealed to us and to our children.
corruption_paragraphs: The doctrine is regularly misused at both ends. The mystic takes it to mean that nothing definite can be said of God, so that doctrine is presumption and every confession is a cage; the rationalist takes the same word to mean that God is simply unavailable, so that theology is guesswork. Deuteronomy 29:29 refuses both. There are secret things, and they belong to the LORD; there are revealed things, and they belong to us and to our children, that we may do all the words of this law. Revelation is real, sufficient, and given for obedience, and its sufficiency does not depend on its being exhaustive.

The distinction the older divines drew is between comprehending and apprehending. A man may truly apprehend the sea — see it, sail on it, drown in it — without comprehending it, that is, without containing it. So God is truly known by the believer, in the face of Jesus Christ, and never encompassed. That is why Romans 11:33 stands where it does. Paul's doxology is not a retreat from the argument of chapters 9 to 11 but its summit; a man who has thought as far as he can think and reached the edge is the only man in a position to say the ways are past finding out.

Job 11:7 has a further sting, because Zophar asks the right question for the wrong purpose — he uses God's unsearchableness to shut Job up. That is the pastoral abuse of the doctrine, and it is common: the mystery of God invoked not in worship but to end a conversation, so that a sufferer with a real question is told he is being impertinent. God Himself answers Job out of the whirlwind with seventy questions of His own, and never once tells him he should not have asked.
roots_summary: Hebrew cheqer (H2714), searching out, a thing found by search; en cheqer, unsearchable; Greek anexereunetos (G419), unsearchable; anexichniastos (G421), past tracing out.
roots_lines: Hebrew cheqer (H2714) — searching, investigation; Job 11:7, Isaiah 40:28, Psalm 145:3, Proverbs 25:3.
Greek anexereunetos (G419) — unsearchable; Romans 11:33 only.
Greek anexichniastos (G421) — past finding out, untraceable; Romans 11:33, Ephesians 3:8.
usage: “Canst thou by searching find out God?” — the right question, asked to end an argument.
“How unsearchable are his judgments” — said at the summit of the argument, not instead of it.
“The secret things belong unto the LORD… those things which are revealed belong unto us” — the division that saves the doctrine.

pos: n. (continued existence; the means of living; in theology, the mode of being proper to each Person of the Trinity)
etymology: Latin subsistere, to stand firm, to remain. The confessions use it in the technical sense: three subsistences in one divine Being — the Latin rendering of the Greek hupostasis.
biblical_def: In its ordinary sense subsistence is continued being, and Scripture grounds all of it outside the creature: “by him all things consist” (Col 1:17); He is “upholding all things by the word of his power” (Heb 1:3); “in him we live, and move, and have our being” (Act 17:28). In its technical sense the word names the three Persons: the Confession says that in the divine and infinite Being there are three subsistences, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, of one substance, power and eternity. Hebrews uses the underlying Greek of the Son as “the express image of his person” (Heb 1:3), and the Lord commands baptism into one name held by three (Mat 28:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines subsistence as real being; existence; competent provision for the support of life; and, in theology, that which underlies accidents, the personal subsistence in the Godhead.
webster_full: SUBSISTENCE, n. Real being; as a chain of differences and subsistences.
2. Competent provision for the support of life; means of supporting life.
3. Inherence; as the subsistence of qualities in bodies.
4. In theology, that which underlies all accidents; the personal subsistence in the Godhead.
scriptures: Col 1:17
And he is before all things, and by him all things consist.
Heb 1:3

Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high;
For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring.
Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
Neither is worshipped with men's hands, as though he needed any thing, seeing he giveth to all life, and breath, and all things;
corruption_summary: Creation is thought to run on its own once wound up, and Colossians says that by Him all things consist, present tense.
corruption_paragraphs: Deism is the belief that God made the world and left it running, and it survives in ordinary Christian imagination long after it has been formally denied: the universe operates by its laws, and God is consulted when the laws fail. Colossians 1:17 and Hebrews 1:3 describe something else entirely. All things consist — hold together, cohere — in Him, and He is at this moment upholding all things by the word of His power. The laws of nature are the ordinary manner of that upholding, not an alternative to it, and if the word were withdrawn there would be no residue of physics left running.

The pastoral consequence is immediate. Providence is not God's occasional intervention in a self-sufficient system; it is the continuation of the same act by which the thing was made. That is why Scripture can attribute the sparrow's fall and the number of a man's hairs to the Father without embarrassment, and why Acts 17:25 says He giveth to all life, and breath, and all things — the breath being taken now, as this sentence is read, is a gift and not a possession.

In the technical sense the word guards the Trinity from two collapses. If the three are only names for one Person appearing in turn, the Son's prayer to the Father is a performance and Gethsemane is theatre; if they are three beings, there are three gods. Subsistence says that the distinction is real and eternal and is not a distinction of essence: the Father is not the Son, and there is one God. The word is technical because the alternatives are heresies, and every generation that grows impatient with the vocabulary rediscovers the heresies within about a decade.
roots_summary: Greek sunistemi (G4921), to hold together, consist; phero (G5342), to bear, uphold; hupostasis (G5287), substance, person, subsistence.
roots_lines: Greek sunistemi (G4921) — to consist, hold together; Colossians 1:17, 2 Peter 3:5.
Greek phero (G5342) — to uphold, bear; Hebrews 1:3.
Greek hupostasis (G5287) — person, substance; Hebrews 1:3, 11:1, 2 Corinthians 9:4.
usage: “By him all things consist” — present tense, and continuous.
“Upholding all things by the word of his power” — the laws are the manner, not the alternative.
“The express image of his person” — the word the confessions build the doctrine on.

pos: adj. (incapable of failing or deceiving; certain; rendering Greek tekmerion in the phrase infallible proofs)
etymology: Latin in, not, and fallere, to deceive, to fail. The Greek of Acts 1:3, tekmerion, is a proof that settles a matter beyond dispute, as against a mere sign.
biblical_def: The word occurs once: the risen Lord “shewed himself alive after his passion by many infallible proofs, being seen of them forty days” (Act 1:3). The property belongs to God's word: “the scripture cannot be broken” (John 10:35); “All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine” (2Ti 3:16); “the law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple” (Psa 19:7). And it belongs to God's purpose: “My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure” (Isa 46:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines infallible as not fallible; not capable of erring; exempt from liability to mistake; certain; not liable to fail or deceive; certain to produce the effect.
webster_full: INFALLIBLE, a. Not fallible; not capable of erring; entirely exempt from liability to mistake; applied to persons.
2. Not liable to fail, or to deceive confidence; certain; as infallible evidence; infallible success.
3. Certain to produce a particular effect.
scriptures: Act 1:3
To whom also he shewed himself alive after his passion by many infallible proofs, being seen of them forty days, and speaking of the things pertaining to the kingdom of God:
John 10:35
If he called them gods, unto whom the word of God came, and the scripture cannot be broken;
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
Psa 19:7
The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple.
Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure:
corruption_summary: Infallibility is claimed for a man and denied to the book, and Scripture attaches it to the word, the counsel, and the proofs of the resurrection.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome locates infallibility in a living voice, on the argument that a book cannot interpret itself and a church must therefore be able to speak without error. The Reformed answer is that the property belongs to God's speech and not to any successor's: the scripture cannot be broken, said the Lord, resting an argument on a single word of a psalm; the law of the LORD is perfect; and the sufficiency of that word is what makes an infallible interpreter unnecessary. The claim of 1870 also has a historical difficulty its defenders have never resolved, in the sixth-century condemnation of Honorius by a council the same church calls ecumenical.

The liberal error is to concede infallibility to the church, to conscience, to scholarship, or to the age — to anything except the text. It is worth noticing that the concession is never a reduction in the number of infallible authorities; it is a transfer. Every man has a final court, and if it is not the Scripture it will be his own judgment wearing an academic gown. The Confession's phrase is the infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture itself, which locates both the authority and its limits in one place.

Acts 1:3 keeps the word from floating free of evidence. The proofs of the resurrection are called infallible — the Greek is the term for a demonstration that settles the case — and they were empirical: forty days, many appearances, eating and drinking, wounds offered to a doubter's hand. Christianity does not ask for a leap in the dark; it asks for belief on testimony, which is how nearly everything else a man knows was learned, and the testimony is of a kind Luke was willing to call proof.
roots_summary: Greek tekmerion (G5039), a sure sign, a demonstrative proof; luo (G3089), to loose, break, of the scripture; theopneustos (G2315), God-breathed.
roots_lines: Greek tekmerion (G5039) — infallible proof; Acts 1:3 only.
Greek ou dunatai luthenai (G3089) — cannot be broken; John 10:35.
Greek theopneustos (G2315) — given by inspiration of God; 2 Timothy 3:16 only.
usage: “Many infallible proofs” — the Greek is a demonstration that settles the case.
“The scripture cannot be broken” — an argument rested on a single word.
“My counsel shall stand” — the other thing that cannot fail.

pos: adj. (heavenly; belonging to the heavens; rendering Greek epouranios)
etymology: Latin caelestis, from caelum, heaven. Paul's Greek is epouranios, upon-heavenly, the word he uses for the heavenly places and the heavenly Man.
biblical_def: Paul answers the question “how are the dead raised up? and with what body do they come?” by an argument from kinds: “There are also celestial bodies, and bodies terrestrial: but the glory of the celestial is one, and the glory of the terrestrial is another” (1Co 15:40). The resurrection body belongs to the first kind: “As is the earthy, such are they also that are earthy: and as is the heavenly, such are they also that are heavenly. And as we have borne the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly” (1Co 15:48–49), for Christ “shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body” (Php 3:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines celestial as heavenly; pertaining to the superior regions or heaven; belonging to the spiritual heaven; and, as a noun, an inhabitant of heaven.
webster_full: CELESTIAL, a. Heavenly; belonging or relating to heaven; dwelling in heaven; as celestial spirits; celestial regions.
2. Belonging to the upper regions, or visible heaven; as celestial signs; the celestial globe.
3. Heavenly; supremely excellent.
CELESTIAL, n. An inhabitant of heaven.
scriptures: There are also celestial bodies, and bodies terrestrial: but the glory of the celestial is one, and the glory of the terrestrial is another.
As is the earthy, such are they also that are earthy: and as is the heavenly, such are they also that are heavenly.
And as we have borne the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly.
Php 3:21
Who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body, according to the working whereby he is able even to subdue all things unto himself.
It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body.
corruption_summary: The resurrection body is imagined as a ghost or as the same body returned unchanged, and Paul says it is sown one thing and raised another.
corruption_paragraphs: First Corinthians 15 is written against two errors at once, and both survive. The first is that the resurrection is spiritual only — a survival of the soul, a memory in God, an influence — and Paul answers with a body, seed and plant, terrestrial and celestial, and the flat statement that if Christ be not raised your faith is vain. The second is the crude opposite, that the same body is simply reassembled and resumed, which the chapter's own language forbids: it is sown in corruption and raised in incorruption, sown a natural body and raised a spiritual body.

The word spiritual in verse 44 is the one most often misread. It does not mean immaterial; Paul has spent the chapter insisting on a body, and the risen Christ ate broiled fish. It means a body animated and governed by the Spirit rather than by the soul-life of this age — as durable as the glory it will bear, and no longer subject to the decay that made the first one a seed. The continuity is real, as a wheat plant is continuous with the grain, and so is the transformation.

The practical corruption is a Christianity that has quietly stopped expecting a body at all, and speaks at funerals only of a soul gone to be with the Lord. That is true, and it is the lesser half. The creed's last article but one is the resurrection of the body, and Philippians 3:21 makes it Christ's own work upon this vile body — the one that failed, the one in the ground — fashioned like unto His glorious body. The hope is not escape from the flesh but its redemption.
roots_summary: Greek epouranios (G2032), heavenly, celestial; epigeios (G1919), earthly, terrestrial; soma pneumatikon (G4983, G4152), a spiritual body.
roots_lines: Greek epouranios (G2032) — heavenly, celestial; 1 Corinthians 15:40, 15:48–49, Ephesians 1:3, 2:6, Hebrews 3:1.
Greek epigeios (G1919) — earthly, terrestrial; 1 Corinthians 15:40, 2 Corinthians 5:1, Philippians 3:19.
Greek pneumatikos (G4152) — spiritual; 1 Corinthians 15:44, 15:46.
usage: “The glory of the celestial is one, and the glory of the terrestrial is another” — an argument from kinds.
“We shall also bear the image of the heavenly” — the image changed, the body kept.
“Fashioned like unto his glorious body” — done to this body, not instead of it.

pos: adj. (belonging to time; lasting only for a season; rendering Greek proskairos)
etymology: Latin temporalis, from tempus, time. Paul's Greek, proskairos, is literally for-a-season — the same word used of the stony-ground hearer who endures for a while.
biblical_def: “While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal” (2Co 4:18) — and the verse before gives the exchange: “our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory” (2Co 4:17). The same Greek describes the hearer who has no root and “dureth for a while” (Mat 13:21), and the choice Moses refused: “the pleasures of sin for a season” (Heb 11:25). John states the outcome: “the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever” (1Jn 2:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines temporal as pertaining to this life or this world; secular, not spiritual or ecclesiastical; measured or limited by time; not eternal.
webster_full: TEMPORAL, a. Pertaining to this life or this world or the body only; secular; as temporal concerns; temporal affairs.
2. Measured or limited by time, or by this life or this state of things; having limited existence; not eternal.
3. Not ecclesiastical or spiritual; as temporal power.
scriptures: While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal.
For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory;
Yet hath he not root in himself, but dureth for a while: for when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended.
Choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season;
And the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever.
corruption_summary: The visible is treated as the solid thing and the eternal as the speculation, and Paul calls the visible the temporary one.
corruption_paragraphs: Second Corinthians 4:18 reverses the ordinary estimate of reality. The things which are seen — the body, the money, the house, the affliction, the empire — are the temporal ones; the things which are not seen are eternal. Every practical decision a man makes assumes one ranking or the other, and the modern instinct is to call the visible realistic and the invisible a comfort. Paul, writing with a wasting body and a list of beatings behind him, calls the beatings light and momentary, and he is not being brave: he is doing arithmetic with the correct values.

The word's other use is a warning about religion that is real and shallow. The stony-ground hearer receives the word with joy and dureth for a while, the same root — his faith is temporal, keyed to a season, and when tribulation ariseth because of the word he is offended. Hebrews 11:25 puts the same adjective on sin's side of the ledger: Moses chose affliction with the people of God rather than the pleasures of sin for a season, and the choice was rational because one term was short.

In the older controversies temporal also meant secular, and the phrase temporal power named the claim of the church to civil rule. The Reformed have generally held the two spheres distinct: the magistrate bears the sword, the church bears the keys, and neither should borrow the other's instrument. A church that reaches for temporal power usually gets it and then discovers that it has exchanged the thing that is eternal for the thing Paul said was passing.
roots_summary: Greek proskairos (G4340), for a season, temporary; aionios (G166), eternal; parago (G3855), to pass away.
roots_lines: Greek proskairos (G4340) — temporal, for a season; 2 Corinthians 4:18, Matthew 13:21, Mark 4:17, Hebrews 11:25.
Greek aionios (G166) — eternal; 2 Corinthians 4:17–18, Matthew 25:46, John 3:16.
Greek parago (G3855) — to pass away; 1 John 2:17, 1 Corinthians 7:31.
usage: “The things which are seen are temporal” — the visible is the temporary one.
“Dureth for a while” — the same word, of a faith with no root.
“The pleasures of sin for a season” — the term that made Moses' choice rational.

pos: v. (repealed, annulled by authority; used of the ceremonial law under the new covenant)
etymology: Latin abrogare, to repeal a law by the vote of the people — ab, away, and rogare, to propose a law. A law abrogated is not broken but withdrawn by the authority that gave it.
biblical_def: To be abrogated is to be repealed by the lawgiver. Hebrews says of the priestly commandment, “there is verily a disannulling of the commandment going before for the weakness and unprofitableness thereof” (Heb 7:18), and of the first covenant, “in that he saith, A new covenant, he hath made the first old. Now that which decayeth and waxeth old is ready to vanish away” (Heb 8:13). Paul: Christ has abolished “in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances” (Eph 2:15), “blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us… nailing it to his cross” (Col 2:14). The moral law is not among them: “Do we then make void the law through faith? God forbid: yea, we establish the law” (Rom 3:31).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines abrogate as to repeal; to annul by an authoritative act; to abolish by the authority of the maker or his successor.
webster_full: ABROGATE, v.t. To repeal; to annul by an authoritative act; to abolish by the authority of the maker or his successor; applied to the repeal of laws, decrees, ordinances, the abolition of established customs, &c.
scriptures: Heb 7:18
For there is verily a disannulling of the commandment going before for the weakness and unprofitableness thereof.
Heb 8:13
In that he saith, A new covenant, he hath made the first old. Now that which decayeth and waxeth old is ready to vanish away.
Eph 2:15
Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances; for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace;
Col 2:14
Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, which was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross;
Rom 3:31
Do we then make void the law through faith? God forbid: yea, we establish the law.
corruption_summary: The whole law is declared abrogated or none of it is, and the Confession distinguishes the ceremonial, the judicial and the moral.
corruption_paragraphs: Everything turns on what was repealed. The Reformed division is threefold: the ceremonial law, which pointed forward and is abrogated in Christ; the judicial law given to Israel as a body politic, which expired with that state, though its general equity may still instruct a magistrate; and the moral law, summarised in the ten commandments, which the Confession says doth for ever bind all, justified persons as well as others. Romans 3:31 is the hinge: do we make void the law through faith? God forbid; yea, we establish the law. Faith does not repeal the standard; it satisfies it in Christ and then writes it on the heart.

The antinomian collapse takes Colossians 2:14 to have nailed the whole law to the cross, and reads any appeal to a commandment as a return to bondage. But the handwriting of ordinances that was against us is a debt-note, not a moral standard, and Paul who wrote it also told children to honour father and mother because it is the first commandment with promise. The Judaising collapse runs the other way, reinstating what Hebrews says is ready to vanish away — feasts, food laws, a priesthood, a temple — and Galatians is the letter written against it.

Hebrews 8:13 has a note of tenderness that is easy to miss. That which decayeth and waxeth old is ready to vanish away: the old covenant is described as an aged thing near its end, not as an enemy destroyed. It served, it pointed, and it is honoured in its passing. Christians who speak of the Old Testament with contempt have misread the tone as well as the doctrine, and Hebrews spends its whole length proving the new by the reverent exposition of the old.
roots_summary: Greek athetesis (G115), a setting aside, disannulling; katargeo (G2673), to render inoperative, abolish; exaleipho (G1813), to blot out; palaioo (G3822), to make or become old.
roots_lines: Greek athetesis (G115) — disannulling, putting away; Hebrews 7:18, 9:26.
Greek katargeo (G2673) — to abolish, make of none effect; Ephesians 2:15, 2 Timothy 1:10, 2 Corinthians 3:13.
Greek exaleipho (G1813) — to blot out; Colossians 2:14, Acts 3:19; palaioo (G3822), Hebrews 8:13.
usage: “A disannulling of the commandment going before” — repealed by the Lawgiver, not broken.
“Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us” — a debt-note, not a standard.
“Yea, we establish the law” — the hinge the antinomian must get past.

pos: adj. (given freely, without price and without cause in the receiver)
etymology: Latin gratuitus, free, from gratia, favour. The Reformers' standing phrase is gratuitous justification — a righteousness given for nothing, and the Authorized Version's word for it is freely.
biblical_def: A gratuitous gift is one with no price and no cause in the receiver. Paul: “being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Rom 3:24) — the Greek adverb means as a gift, for nothing, and is the same word the Lord uses in “freely ye have received, freely give” (Mat 10:8). The invitation keeps the term: “Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price” (Isa 55:1); and the last page of Scripture, “whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely” (Rev 22:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines gratuitous as free; voluntary; not required by justice; given without an equivalent; asserted or taken without proof.
webster_full: GRATUITOUS, a. Free; voluntary; not required by justice; granted without claim or merit; as a gratuitous payment.
2. Asserted or taken without proof; as a gratuitous assumption.
scriptures: Rom 3:24
Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus:
Mat 10:8
Heal the sick, cleanse the lepers, raise the dead, cast out devils: freely ye have received, freely give.
Isa 55:1
Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.
And the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely.
Rom 5:15

But not as the offence, so also is the free gift. For if through the offence of one many be dead, much more the grace of God, and the gift by grace, which is by one man, Jesus Christ, hath abounded unto many.
corruption_summary: Grace is offered on terms, and the Greek adverb behind justified freely is the word for what is given as a gift and costs the receiver nothing.
corruption_paragraphs: The Greek word in Romans 3:24 is dorean, and its plainest use in the New Testament is John 15:25, where it is translated without a cause: they hated me without a cause. Set the two verses together and the doctrine is exact. Christ was hated gratuitously — for no reason in Him — and the sinner is justified gratuitously, for no reason in him. In both directions the cause lies outside the person it falls on, and that is what the Reformers meant by gratuitous justification: not that it cost nothing, since it cost the blood, but that it cost the receiver nothing and was earned by nothing in him.

The corruption is never a flat denial; it is the quiet addition of a term. Grace is free, and you must be sincere; free, and you must persevere in order to have deserved it; free, and there is a small charge for the sacraments, the indulgence, the pledge, the level of commitment. Isaiah 55:1 was written against every such tariff, and the strangest word in it is buy: come ye, buy, and eat, without money and without price. The sinner comes as a purchaser to a market where the price has been paid, and the only qualification named in the verse is thirst.

The abuse on the other side is to conclude that a gift costing the receiver nothing therefore asks nothing of him. Matthew 10:8 refuses it in five words: freely ye have received, freely give. The gratuitous character of the gift is the pattern for the disciple's whole conduct with it — he was healed for nothing and heals for nothing, was forgiven a debt he could not pay and forgives a hundred pence. A man who has genuinely received gratuitously becomes recognisable, and the sign is not what he has stopped doing but what he has stopped charging for.
roots_summary: Greek dorean (G1432), freely, as a gift, without cause; charis (G5485), grace; dorea (G1431), a free gift; Hebrew chinnam (H2600), for nothing, without price.
roots_lines: Greek dorean (G1432) — freely, as a gift; Romans 3:24, Matthew 10:8, Revelation 21:6, 22:17; and without a cause, John 15:25.
Greek dorea (G1431) — a free gift; Romans 5:15, 5:17, Ephesians 3:7, Acts 2:38.
Hebrew chinnam (H2600) — for nought, without price; Isaiah 52:3, 55:1, Genesis 29:15.
usage: “Justified freely by his grace” — the same word rendered without a cause when they hated Him.
“Buy wine and milk without money and without price” — a purchase where the only qualification is thirst.
“Freely ye have received, freely give” — the gift becomes the pattern.
